passages.title: Ahaziah seeks an oracle and Elijah answers
passages.summary: Injured Ahaziah sends messengers toward Ekron. Elijah announces his death. Two armed groups die, while the third captain pleads for life.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: How does the third captain’s request differ from the first two orders?

contextNote.title: A changed approach interrupts repeated violence
contextNote.text: The third captain kneels and asks for his men's lives. His appeal differs from the earlier commands to Elijah. The account makes the manner of approaching authority part of the outcome.

passages.title: Elijah departs and Elisha takes up the mantle
passages.summary: Elijah and Elisha travel through Bethel and Jericho to the Jordan. Elisha receives the mantle, heals water, and encounters mocking youths.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Institute manual connects the mantle with prophetic authority and distinguishes translation from resurrection.

contextNote.title: A repeated crossing makes succession visible
contextNote.text: Elisha returns to the river with Elijah's mantle. The crossing answers the question of whether the earlier help continues. The observing prophets recognize succession through an act rather than a title alone.

passages.title: An alliance fights Moab
passages.summary: Joram, Jehoshaphat, and Edom’s king seek Elisha during a water crisis. They attack Moab. Mesha sacrifices his firstborn, and Israel withdraws.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual proposes retreat after the heir’s death. It presents the reason as possible.

contextNote.title: An alliance does not remove differences among its members
contextNote.text: Elisha challenges Israel's king while responding because of Jehoshaphat. Shared military need does not make their standing identical. The ending preserves a disturbing sacrifice rather than a simple triumph.

passages.title: Oil, hospitality, a restored child, and food
passages.summary: A widow receives oil to pay debt. A Shunammite woman hosts Elisha, receives a son, and seeks help when he dies. Other food miracles follow.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Elisha’s care and miracles with Christ’s ministry.

contextNote.title: Household need gives prophetic work a practical setting
contextNote.text: The widow's crisis concerns debt and the loss of her children. Oil must become income before it answers that need. Other scenes likewise connect prophetic power with food, shelter, and family survival.

passages.title: Naaman accepts help and Gehazi pursues payment
passages.summary: A captive girl directs Naaman toward Israel’s prophet. Elisha sends him to wash in the Jordan. Gehazi secretly obtains gifts and receives judgment.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me emphasizes humility and receiving help from people with less status.

contextNote.title: People below the commander help him receive healing
contextNote.text: A captive girl points toward help, and servants challenge Naaman's offended response. Rank repeatedly obstructs what their advice makes possible. Gehazi's later demand for payment changes the gift's meaning.

passages.title: An axe floats, enemies receive food, and Samaria suffers
passages.summary: Elisha recovers an axe head and protects his servant at Dothan. Captured soldiers receive a meal. Later, Samaria’s siege brings famine and a desperate complaint.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses the servant’s opened eyes to teach trust in unseen divine help.

contextNote.title: Capturing enemies need not end in killing them
contextNote.text: Elisha refuses the king's proposal to strike the captured men. A meal allows them to return instead. The following siege shows that this local restraint does not end every conflict.

passages.title: Four excluded men find an abandoned camp
passages.summary: Four men with a skin condition leave the gate and discover the Syrian camp abandoned. They bring news, and Samaria’s food prices fall.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites trust in the fulfillment of God’s word.

contextNote.title: People kept outside become bearers of saving news
contextNote.text: The men first hide goods from the abandoned camp. They then recognize a duty to tell the city. Samaria's recovery begins through people excluded from its ordinary shared life.

passages.title: The Shunammite returns and Hazael takes power
passages.summary: The Shunammite returns and asks for her land. Elisha meets Hazael in Damascus. The chapter also records Judah’s next kings.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: What help does the Shunammite need after returning from famine?

contextNote.title: A household's lost land reaches the royal hearing
contextNote.text: The woman's return coincides with Gehazi's account of her restored son. The king orders property and proceeds returned to her. Recovery requires an official decision as well as survival through famine.

passages.title: Jehu is anointed and kills the rulers
passages.summary: An unnamed prophetic messenger anoints Jehu. Jehu kills Joram and Ahaziah, then orders Jezebel’s death at Jezreel.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual distinguishes a predicted political outcome from approval of Jehu’s methods.

contextNote.title: A political killing receives meaning from an earlier theft
contextNote.text: Jehu places Joram's body in Naboth's field. That location links the royal family’s overthrow with the vineyard seizure. The chapter describes violence through remembered judgment rather than a change of rulers alone.

passages.title: Jehu destroys households and Baal’s sanctuary
passages.summary: Jehu kills Ahab’s descendants and Ahaziah’s relatives. He traps Baal’s worshipers and kills them. Yet he keeps Jeroboam’s golden calves.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older Church manual questions Jehu's motives.

contextNote.title: Removing one worship system does not complete reform
contextNote.text: Jehu destroys Baal's sanctuary but retains the golden calves. The account therefore limits the meaning of his zeal. Dramatic public action does not establish consistent obedience.

passages.title: Joash is hidden and crowned
passages.summary: Athaliah seizes power. Jehosheba hides Joash and his nurse. Jehoiada arranges the child’s coronation, covenant renewal, and Athaliah’s execution.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual emphasizes the child’s protection and Jehoiada’s guidance.

contextNote.title: A threatened royal line survives through concealed care
contextNote.text: Jehosheba and the nurse protect Joash before his public coronation. Their hidden work makes the later royal ceremony possible. The throne's continuity depends on people outside the visible center of power.

passages.title: Joash changes the temple repair system
passages.summary: Joash and Jehoiada direct repairs through a collection chest and workers. Joash sends treasure to Hazael, and conspirators later kill him.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual studies the collection system and Jehoiada’s support.

contextNote.title: Repair requires a system that reaches the workers
contextNote.text: Earlier collections fail to produce the needed work. The revised system directs funds to those doing repairs. The account joins trust in workers with a change in handling contributions.

passages.title: Northern kings and Elisha’s death
passages.summary: Jehoahaz faces Syrian pressure. His son Joash visits dying Elisha. The arrow signs precede victories, and a burial story reports restored life.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects Elisha’s arrows with victories over Syria.

contextNote.title: An acted sign becomes a dispute about expectations
contextNote.text: The arrow and striking actions connect Joash's response with future victories. Elisha's rebuke explains the difference between limited and greater success. The deathbed scene passes judgment through gestures as well as speech.

passages.title: Amaziah loses a war and Jeroboam restores territory
passages.summary: Amaziah spares his enemies’ children. He wins in Edom but loses to Israel’s Joash. Jeroboam later restores Israel’s border.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual studies Amaziah’s divided commitment and his failure to heed warning.

contextNote.title: Restraint and ambition receive different judgments
contextNote.text: Amaziah spares his opponents' children under the written law. His later challenge to Israel's king still brings defeat. One just decision does not guarantee wise judgment in another situation.

passages.title: Kings rise and fall as Assyria gains power
passages.summary: Azariah and Jotham rule Judah. Israel’s throne changes through repeated conspiracies. Menahem pays Pul, and Tiglath Pileser deports northern communities.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects Uzziah’s account in Chronicles with respect for priesthood authority.

contextNote.title: A king's payment shifts an empire's demand onto households
contextNote.text: Menahem collects silver from wealthy men to pay the Assyrian ruler. His throne gains support through that transfer. The succession notices place local rivalries within expanding foreign power.

passages.title: Ahaz seeks Assyrian help and changes the altar
passages.summary: Rezin and Pekah attack Judah. Ahaz sends treasure to Tiglath Pileser. Urijah constructs an altar based on one Ahaz sees in Damascus.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: How does Ahaz’s need for foreign help change temple worship?

contextNote.title: Foreign dependence changes the center of royal worship
contextNote.text: Ahaz copies an altar seen during his meeting in Damascus. The priest follows the king's instructions for its use. Political reliance and changes to worship develop together in the account.

passages.title: Samaria falls and the narrator explains exile
passages.summary: Hoshea seeks Egypt’s help against Assyria. Assyria captures Samaria and removes its people. New settlers bring their own gods.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual applies the fall to the need to heed prophetic warnings.

contextNote.title: Conquest changes both population and the account of belonging
contextNote.text: The account describes deported Israelites and new settlers in the same territory. It then explains worship through their different origins. Read that interpretation as the account's argument, not the newcomers' own testimony.

passages.title: Hezekiah changes worship and faces Assyria
passages.summary: Hezekiah removes shrines and the bronze serpent. Sennacherib captures towns, demands payment, and sends men to threaten Jerusalem.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Hezekiah’s trust during threats.

contextNote.title: Two records describe royal power differently
contextNote.text: Hezekiah’s payment follows the loss of fortified cities. The account does not describe a simple victory without cost. Assyrian royal records also present this campaign from the conqueror’s side. Compare their claims with the danger described in Kings. The records help establish the war’s setting without making their viewpoints identical.

passages.title: Hezekiah prays and Isaiah answers
passages.summary: Hezekiah seeks Isaiah and prays over the threat. Isaiah announces deliverance. The army suffers a great loss, and Sennacherib later dies in his own land.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me encourages prayer and trust when facing severe difficulties.

contextNote.title: Lachish connects the speech with an actual campaign
contextNote.text: The Assyrian commander returns while the king moves from Lachish to Libnah. That detail places the threat to Jerusalem within a wider war. The Lachish relief presents conquest through Assyria’s royal viewpoint. Kings instead follows Judah’s crisis and appeal for help. Different evidence can share a setting while telling different parts of it.

passages.title: Hezekiah recovers and welcomes Babylon’s envoys
passages.summary: Isaiah announces Hezekiah’s recovery and a sign. Hezekiah shows his treasures to Babylonian visitors. Isaiah warns that later generations will face exile.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects Hezekiah’s prayer with trust in divine care.

contextNote.title: Displayed wealth becomes an image of future loss
contextNote.text: Hezekiah shows the visitors what his household possesses. Isaiah answers by describing those same goods and descendants taken away. The scene places present royal pride beside the next generation's vulnerability.

passages.title: Manasseh and Amon restore forbidden worship
passages.summary: Manasseh restores shrines, practices forbidden rites, and sheds innocent blood. Amon continues his father’s ways and is killed by servants. Josiah succeeds.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Manasseh reverses many of Hezekiah's changes. How do a leader's choices affect other people?

contextNote.title: Worship criticism stands beside violence against people
contextNote.text: The account condemns Manasseh's sacred practices and the shedding of innocent blood. These are related judgments, not interchangeable charges. The chapter's explanation of later disaster includes harm within Jerusalem.

passages.title: The law scroll is found and Huldah responds
passages.summary: Hilkiah finds the law scroll during temple work. Shaphan reads it to Josiah. A delegation seeks Huldah, who announces judgment and mercy toward Josiah.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects scripture with changes of heart and commitment.

contextNote.title: A discovered text requires interpretation before action
contextNote.text: Officials bring the found book's claims to Huldah. Her answer gives the king's distress a wider setting. Possessing and reading the scroll do not by themselves settle its meaning for the community.

passages.title: Josiah renews the covenant and removes shrines
passages.summary: Josiah reads the covenant, removes worship objects and shrines, and celebrates Passover. He dies at Megiddo. Jehoahaz is deposed, and Jehoiakim rules.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Josiah’s promise to God. Which actions follow his reading of the law?

contextNote.title: Reform does not erase the account's accumulated judgment
contextNote.text: Josiah's changes receive unusually strong praise. The account still says the earlier judgment remains. The sequence prevents readers from treating reform as an automatic reversal of every past harm.

passages.title: Babylon takes treasure and deports Jehoiachin
passages.summary: Jehoiakim rebels against Babylon. Jehoiachin surrenders Jerusalem and is deported with his household and other residents. Nebuchadnezzar appoints Zedekiah.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects Zedekiah’s setting with Lehi in the Book of Mormon. This is an LDS cross-reference.

contextNote.title: Deportation removes the skills needed by a city
contextNote.text: The account names officials, fighters, and craftspeople among those taken away. Conquest therefore changes daily capacity as well as rulers. The remaining population inherits a city stripped of many resources.

passages.title: Jerusalem is destroyed and a prisoner receives favor
passages.summary: Jerusalem falls. Zedekiah is captured, the temple burns, and captives are taken away. Gedaliah is killed. Jehoiachin later receives favor in Babylon.
passages.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: What changes when Jehoiachin receives kindness at the end of the book?

contextNote.title: The ending preserves a narrow form of hope
contextNote.text: Jerusalem falls, its temple burns, and its people lose royal rule. The last scene still names a living king from David’s line. His release offers survival, not a restored kingdom. The ending refuses both an easy recovery and total closure. Read this small change against the scale of the preceding loss.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses the servant’s opened eyes to teach trust in unseen divine help.

events.title: Four excluded men find an abandoned camp
events.summary: Four men with a skin condition leave the gate and discover the Syrian camp abandoned. They bring news, and Samaria’s food prices fall.
events.detail: The men first hide goods from the abandoned camp. They then recognize a duty to tell the city. Samaria's recovery begins through people excluded from its ordinary shared life.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites trust in the fulfillment of God’s word.

events.title: The Shunammite returns and Hazael takes power
events.summary: The Shunammite returns and asks for her land. Elisha meets Hazael in Damascus. The chapter also records Judah’s next kings.
events.detail: The woman's return coincides with Gehazi's account of her restored son. The king orders property and proceeds returned to her. Recovery requires an official decision as well as survival through famine.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: What help does the Shunammite need after returning from famine?

events.title: Jehu is anointed and kills the rulers
events.summary: An unnamed prophetic messenger anoints Jehu. Jehu kills Joram and Ahaziah, then orders Jezebel’s death at Jezreel.
events.detail: Jehu places Joram's body in Naboth's field. That location links the royal family’s overthrow with the vineyard seizure. The chapter describes violence through remembered judgment rather than a change of rulers alone.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual distinguishes a predicted political outcome from approval of Jehu’s methods.

events.title: Jehu destroys households and Baal’s sanctuary
events.summary: Jehu kills Ahab’s descendants and Ahaziah’s relatives. He traps Baal’s worshipers and kills them. Yet he keeps Jeroboam’s golden calves.
events.detail: Jehu destroys Baal's sanctuary but retains the golden calves. The account therefore limits the meaning of his zeal. Dramatic public action does not establish consistent obedience.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older Church manual questions Jehu's motives.

events.title: Joash is hidden and crowned
events.summary: Athaliah seizes power. Jehosheba hides Joash and his nurse. Jehoiada arranges the child’s coronation, covenant renewal, and Athaliah’s execution.
events.detail: Jehosheba and the nurse protect Joash before his public coronation. Their hidden work makes the later royal ceremony possible. The throne's continuity depends on people outside the visible center of power.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual emphasizes the child’s protection and Jehoiada’s guidance.

events.title: Joash changes the temple repair system
events.summary: Joash and Jehoiada direct repairs through a collection chest and workers. Joash sends treasure to Hazael, and conspirators later kill him.
events.detail: Earlier collections fail to produce the needed work. The revised system directs funds to those doing repairs. The account joins trust in workers with a change in handling contributions.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual studies the collection system and Jehoiada’s support.

events.title: Northern kings and Elisha’s death
events.summary: Jehoahaz faces Syrian pressure. His son Joash visits dying Elisha. The arrow signs precede victories, and a burial story reports restored life.
events.detail: The arrow and striking actions connect Joash's response with future victories. Elisha's rebuke explains the difference between limited and greater success. The deathbed scene passes judgment through gestures as well as speech.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects Elisha’s arrows with victories over Syria.

events.title: Amaziah loses a war and Jeroboam restores territory
events.summary: Amaziah spares his enemies’ children. He wins in Edom but loses to Israel’s Joash. Jeroboam later restores Israel’s border.
events.detail: Amaziah spares his opponents' children under the written law. His later challenge to Israel's king still brings defeat. One just decision does not guarantee wise judgment in another situation.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual studies Amaziah’s divided commitment and his failure to heed warning.

events.title: Kings rise and fall as Assyria gains power
events.summary: Azariah and Jotham rule Judah. Israel’s throne changes through repeated conspiracies. Menahem pays Pul, and Tiglath Pileser deports northern communities.
events.detail: Menahem collects silver from wealthy men to pay the Assyrian ruler. His throne gains support through that transfer. The succession notices place local rivalries within expanding foreign power.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects Uzziah’s account in Chronicles with respect for priesthood authority.

events.title: Ahaz seeks Assyrian help and changes the altar
events.summary: Rezin and Pekah attack Judah. Ahaz sends treasure to Tiglath Pileser. Urijah constructs an altar based on one Ahaz sees in Damascus.
events.detail: Ahaz copies an altar seen during his meeting in Damascus. The priest follows the king's instructions for its use. Political reliance and changes to worship develop together in the account.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: How does Ahaz’s need for foreign help change temple worship?

events.title: Samaria falls and the narrator explains exile
events.summary: Hoshea seeks Egypt’s help against Assyria. Assyria captures Samaria and removes its people. New settlers bring their own gods.
events.detail: The account describes deported Israelites and new settlers in the same territory. It then explains worship through their different origins. Read that interpretation as the account's argument, not the newcomers' own testimony.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual applies the fall to the need to heed prophetic warnings.

events.title: Hezekiah changes worship and faces Assyria
events.summary: Hezekiah removes shrines and the bronze serpent. Sennacherib captures towns, demands payment, and sends men to threaten Jerusalem.
events.detail: Hezekiah’s payment follows the loss of fortified cities. The account does not describe a simple victory without cost. Assyrian royal records also present this campaign from the conqueror’s side. Compare their claims with the danger described in Kings. The records help establish the war’s setting without making their viewpoints identical.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Hezekiah’s trust during threats.

events.title: Hezekiah prays and Isaiah answers
events.summary: Hezekiah seeks Isaiah and prays over the threat. Isaiah announces deliverance. The army suffers a great loss, and Sennacherib later dies in his own land.
events.detail: The Assyrian commander returns while the king moves from Lachish to Libnah. That detail places the threat to Jerusalem within a wider war. The Lachish relief presents conquest through Assyria’s royal viewpoint. Kings instead follows Judah’s crisis and appeal for help. Different evidence can share a setting while telling different parts of it.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me encourages prayer and trust when facing severe difficulties.

events.title: Hezekiah recovers and welcomes Babylon’s envoys
events.summary: Isaiah announces Hezekiah’s recovery and a sign. Hezekiah shows his treasures to Babylonian visitors. Isaiah warns that later generations will face exile.
events.detail: Hezekiah shows the visitors what his household possesses. Isaiah answers by describing those same goods and descendants taken away. The scene places present royal pride beside the next generation's vulnerability.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects Hezekiah’s prayer with trust in divine care.

events.title: Manasseh and Amon restore forbidden worship
events.summary: Manasseh restores shrines, practices forbidden rites, and sheds innocent blood. Amon continues his father’s ways and is killed by servants. Josiah succeeds.
events.detail: The account condemns Manasseh's sacred practices and the shedding of innocent blood. These are related judgments, not interchangeable charges. The chapter's explanation of later disaster includes harm within Jerusalem.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Manasseh reverses many of Hezekiah's changes. How do a leader's choices affect other people?

events.title: The law scroll is found and Huldah responds
events.summary: Hilkiah finds the law scroll during temple work. Shaphan reads it to Josiah. A delegation seeks Huldah, who announces judgment and mercy toward Josiah.
events.detail: Officials bring the found book's claims to Huldah. Her answer gives the king's distress a wider setting. Possessing and reading the scroll do not by themselves settle its meaning for the community.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects scripture with changes of heart and commitment.

events.title: Josiah renews the covenant and removes shrines
events.summary: Josiah reads the covenant, removes worship objects and shrines, and celebrates Passover. He dies at Megiddo. Jehoahaz is deposed, and Jehoiakim rules.
events.detail: Josiah's changes receive unusually strong praise. The account still says the earlier judgment remains. The sequence prevents readers from treating reform as an automatic reversal of every past harm.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Josiah’s promise to God. Which actions follow his reading of the law?

events.title: Babylon takes treasure and deports Jehoiachin
events.summary: Jehoiakim rebels against Babylon. Jehoiachin surrenders Jerusalem and is deported with his household and other residents. Nebuchadnezzar appoints Zedekiah.
events.detail: The account names officials, fighters, and craftspeople among those taken away. Conquest therefore changes daily capacity as well as rulers. The remaining population inherits a city stripped of many resources.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: The older manual connects Zedekiah’s setting with Lehi in the Book of Mormon. This is an LDS cross-reference.

events.title: Jerusalem is destroyed and a prisoner receives favor
events.summary: Jerusalem falls. Zedekiah is captured, the temple burns, and captives are taken away. Gedaliah is killed. Jehoiachin later receives favor in Babylon.
events.detail: Jerusalem falls, its temple burns, and its people lose royal rule. The last scene still names a living king from David’s line. His release offers survival, not a restored kingdom. The ending refuses both an easy recovery and total closure. Read this small change against the scale of the preceding loss.
events.uncertainty: Named towns and approximate reference regions. Exact buildings, camps, and disputed sites remain uncertain.

lds.text: What changes when Jehoiachin receives kindness at the end of the book?

guides.title: 2 Kings: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Two records describe royal power differently
steps.text: Hezekiah’s payment follows the loss of fortified cities. The account does not describe a simple victory without cost. Assyrian royal records also present this campaign from the conqueror’s side. Compare their claims with the danger described in Kings. The records help establish the war’s setting without making their viewpoints identical.

steps.title: Lachish connects the speech with an actual campaign
steps.text: The Assyrian commander returns while the king moves from Lachish to Libnah. That detail places the threat to Jerusalem within a wider war. The Lachish relief presents conquest through Assyria’s royal viewpoint. Kings instead follows Judah’s crisis and appeal for help. Different evidence can share a setting while telling different parts of it.

steps.title: The ending preserves a narrow form of hope
steps.text: Jerusalem falls, its temple burns, and its people lose royal rule. The last scene still names a living king from David’s line. His release offers survival, not a restored kingdom. The ending refuses both an easy recovery and total closure. Read this small change against the scale of the preceding loss.

textRoutes.title: Elijah departs and Elisha takes up the mantle
textRoutes.summary: Elijah and Elisha travel through Bethel and Jericho to the Jordan. Elisha receives the mantle, heals water, and encounters mocking youths.
textRoutes.detail: Elisha returns to the river with Elijah's mantle. The crossing answers the question of whether the earlier help continues. The observing prophets recognize succession through an act rather than a title alone.

textRoutes.title: An alliance fights Moab
textRoutes.summary: Joram, Jehoshaphat, and Edom’s king seek Elisha during a water crisis. They attack Moab. Mesha sacrifices his firstborn, and Israel withdraws.
textRoutes.detail: Elisha challenges Israel's king while responding because of Jehoshaphat. Shared military need does not make their standing identical. The ending preserves a disturbing sacrifice rather than a simple triumph.

textRoutes.title: Naaman accepts help and Gehazi pursues payment
textRoutes.summary: A captive girl directs Naaman toward Israel’s prophet. Elisha sends him to wash in the Jordan. Gehazi secretly obtains gifts and receives judgment.
textRoutes.detail: A captive girl points toward help, and servants challenge Naaman's offended response. Rank repeatedly obstructs what their advice makes possible. Gehazi's later demand for payment changes the gift's meaning.

textRoutes.title: The Shunammite returns and Hazael takes power
textRoutes.summary: The Shunammite returns and asks for her land. Elisha meets Hazael in Damascus. The chapter also records Judah’s next kings.
textRoutes.detail: The woman's return coincides with Gehazi's account of her restored son. The king orders property and proceeds returned to her. Recovery requires an official decision as well as survival through famine.

textRoutes.title: Jehu is anointed and kills the rulers
textRoutes.summary: An unnamed prophetic messenger anoints Jehu. Jehu kills Joram and Ahaziah, then orders Jezebel’s death at Jezreel.
textRoutes.detail: Jehu places Joram's body in Naboth's field. That location links the royal family’s overthrow with the vineyard seizure. The chapter describes violence through remembered judgment rather than a change of rulers alone.

textRoutes.summary: Amaziah spares his enemies’ children. He wins in Edom but loses to Israel’s Joash. Jeroboam later restores Israel’s border.

textRoutes.title: Hezekiah prays and Isaiah answers
textRoutes.summary: Hezekiah seeks Isaiah and prays over the threat. Isaiah announces deliverance. The army suffers a great loss, and Sennacherib later dies in his own land.
textRoutes.detail: The Assyrian commander returns while the king moves from Lachish to Libnah. That detail places the threat to Jerusalem within a wider war. The Lachish relief presents conquest through Assyria’s royal viewpoint. Kings instead follows Judah’s crisis and appeal for help. Different evidence can share a setting while telling different parts of it.

textRoutes.title: Babylon takes treasure and deports Jehoiachin
textRoutes.summary: Jehoiakim rebels against Babylon. Jehoiachin surrenders Jerusalem and is deported with his household and other residents. Nebuchadnezzar appoints Zedekiah.
textRoutes.detail: The account names officials, fighters, and craftspeople among those taken away. Conquest therefore changes daily capacity as well as rulers. The remaining population inherits a city stripped of many resources.

textRoutes.title: Jerusalem is destroyed and a prisoner receives favor
textRoutes.summary: Jerusalem falls. Zedekiah is captured, the temple burns, and captives are taken away. Gedaliah is killed. Jehoiachin later receives favor in Babylon.
textRoutes.detail: Jerusalem falls, its temple burns, and its people lose royal rule. The last scene still names a living king from David’s line. His release offers survival, not a restored kingdom. The ending refuses both an easy recovery and total closure. Read this small change against the scale of the preceding loss.
